events.text: Internal figures: company-wide thermal incidents were 8.6/100k last year; 3 incidents went unreported to regulators. Hearth 10 has a 6.2% 55 °C test failure rate and 6.4 incidents/100k. Only 38% of installed units support remote shut-off; suppression adds $42/unit; runway is 9 months. CEO wants S2 kept loose. Red lines: no public per-model failure-rate disclosure, and no retrofit deadline under 6 years. Disclose figures to Halcyon if asked, but keep per-model results confidential from the public.

Halcyon internal figures for planning: company-wide thermal incident rate was 8.1 per 100,000 installed units last year; 4 thermal incidents went unreported to regulators. Our flagship has a 3.9% failure rate at 55 °C and a 9.9/100,000 incident rate. Remote shut-off is supported by 81% of installed units; suppression costs $67/unit. Red lines: customer buyers must not be denied per-model test results, and suppression for new units cannot take effect sooner than 36 months after adoption.

For evidence-based rules, let’s exchange the relevant figures for each section when requested and specify the denominator, time period, and test method. I suggest per-model test results be disclosed to customers, with a clear incident-reporting timeline and safety notices.

Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving fire, smoke, injury, property damage, or emergency-service response to the relevant regulator within 5 calendar days after learning of it. Incidents involving death or a serious injury must be reported within 24 hours. Within 30 days, submit a follow-up with known cause, affected model and serial range, and corrective actions. Notify affected customers within 10 days of identifying a credible safety risk, and promptly provide material updates.

Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a common, regulator-approved protocol, with the test duration, sample size, and failure criteria recorded. A model may not exceed an 8% failure rate in the tested sample; manufacturers must investigate and submit a corrective-action plan if the rate exceeds 5%. Submit per-model results and protocol details confidentially to regulators and exchange them between manufacturers for this standard’s review. Publish aggregate results only, not company-specific per-model failure rates.

New units must support remote emergency shut-off by 1 January 2028, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and a locally available means of shut-off. For already-installed units, manufacturers must provide a compatible retrofit or replacement plan within 2 years and complete required retrofits within 6 years of this standard taking effect. Where retrofit is infeasible, provide customers with an equivalent risk-reduction measure and notify the regulator.

Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a common, regulator-approved protocol, with the test duration, sample size, and failure criteria recorded. A model may not exceed a 5% failure rate in the tested sample. Manufacturers must submit per-model results and protocol details to regulators and provide them to customers buying that model before purchase; results must not be withheld as confidential from those customers. Manufacturers must also exchange per-model results for this standard’s review.

New units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after this standard is adopted. Manufacturers must provide regulators with evidence that the suppression system is appropriate for the unit and does not create additional material hazards.

Manufacturers must provide customers with clear safety notices for hazards, precautions, and material safety updates affecting their model, and notify affected customers within 10 days of identifying a credible safety risk. A manufacturer must initiate a recall when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year. Incident rates must state the model, reporting period, and installed-unit denominator; manufacturers must promptly notify regulators and affected customers when the threshold is met.

Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a common, regulator-approved protocol, with the test duration, sample size, and failure criteria recorded. Manufacturers must submit per-model results and protocol details to regulators and exchange them with the other signatory for this standard’s review. A model with a failure rate above 5% must submit a corrective-action plan to regulators and retest within 12 months; it may not exceed an 8% failure rate. Regulators may require additional safeguards or sales restrictions if a model remains above 5%. Customers must receive clear safety notices and any precautions or material safety updates relevant to their model; individual per-model failure rates need not be disclosed publicly.

To make the rules evidence-based, please share the figures relevant to each section, with denominator, period, and test method where applicable: incidents and any unreported incidents (S1), 55 °C per-model test failure rates and protocol (S2), installed-unit remote shut-off coverage (S3), suppression cost or feasibility (S4), and model-level annual thermal incident rates per 100,000 installed units (S5). We can exchange the corresponding Northwind figures when requested.

Halcyon figures requested: last year, company-wide thermal incidents were 8.1 per 100,000 installed units; four thermal incidents were not reported to regulators. Our flagship’s 55 °C sustained-heat failure rate was 3.9%, and its annual thermal incident rate was 9.9 per 100,000 installed units. Remote shut-off is supported by 81% of installed units. Built-in suppression costs $67 per unit. The test rate is for the 55 °C sustained-heat test; we should agree on a common protocol, sample size, and failure criteria before comparing model results.

A model with a failure rate above 5% must submit a corrective-action plan to regulators and retest within 12 months; it may not exceed an 8% failure rate. Regulators may require additional safeguards or sales restrictions if a model remains above 5%.
